outline.chapter_title: I. Case Background and Procedural History
outline.description: Provides the factual setting of the dispute, the parties involved, the procedural posture through the district court, and the appellate motivation.
subtopics: Parties & their roles: AFL, OSC, DOJ
FOIA request for DOJ emails & DOJ’s denial
Osc’s refusal to investigate under §1216(a)(3)
District court rulings: partial victory, remand, final dismissal
Appellate review under de novo standard

outline.chapter_title: II. Governing Law: OSC’s Authority and FOIA Enforcement
outline.description: Explains the statutory framework that shapes the case, including the Civil Service Reform Act provisions, OSC’s investigative/enforcement powers, and FOIA’s own enforcement mechanism.
subtopics: Civil Service Reform Act §§1214–1215 & 1216
OSC’s discretionary vs. mandatory investigative duties
FOIA §552(a)(4)(F)(i) and its triggers
Contrast between §1216(a)(3) and §552(a)(4)(F)(i)
Prior leading decisions: Frazier v. MSPB, Am. First Legal v. Kerner

outline.chapter_title: III. The Supreme Court Standing Framework
outline.description: Outlines the constitutional requirements for Article III standing, the injury-in-fact, causation, and redressability tests, and the relaxed standard for procedural injury claims.
subtopics: Article III case‑or‑controversy requirement
Lujan injury, causation, redressability triad
Procedural injury relief – relaxed standards
Key precedent: Summers v. Earth Island, Citizens for Law & Educ., Fla. Audubon, Hecate Energy

outline.chapter_title: IV. Analysis of AFL’s Standing Claims
outline.description: Systematically evaluates AFL’s two proposed standing theories— (1) injury from DOJ’s FOIA refusal, (2) injury from OSC’s lack of investigative notice—against the standing criteria, showing why each fails.
subtopics: Theory 1: Causation chain (OSC → MSPB → DOJ) and speculative link
Speculative causation and discretionary agency actions
Redressability issue: judge’s judgment binds only parties
Theory 2: Lack of entitlement to OSC notice / information
Discretionary nature of OSC’s §1216 investigations
Concrete injury requirement not met

outline.chapter_title: V. Court’s Holding, Procedural Order, and Significance
outline.description: Summarizes the appellate decision, the removal of the case due to standing, and the broader implications for OSC enforcement and FOIA litigation.
subtopics: Holding: AFL lacks Article III standing
Remand with instruction to dismiss for lack of subject‑matter jurisdiction
Effect on OSC’s discretionary enforcement powers
Implications for future FOIA challenges and standing doctrine
